sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Breast-Conserving Surgery vs Mastectomy: How to Decide
sectionToMerge.intro: Choosing between breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy) and mastectomy is a personal decision that depends on your tumour, breast size, health, and preferences. These FAQs explain how the two operations compare and what to discuss with your surgical and oncology team.

items.q: What is breast-conserving surgery?
items.a: Breast-conserving surgery, also called a lumpectomy or wide local excision, removes the tumour along with a margin of surrounding healthy tissue while keeping most of the breast. It is usually followed by radiation therapy to lower the risk of the cancer returning. This approach may be suitable for selected patients with early-stage or smaller tumours, but the final choice depends on tumour size, location, and specialist review.

items.q: What is a mastectomy?
items.a: A mastectomy is surgery that removes the entire breast, including the tumour and most breast tissue. There are several types, such as total, skin-sparing, and nipple-sparing mastectomy, and reconstruction may be offered at the same time or later. A mastectomy may be considered when tumours are large, involve more than one area, or when radiation is not advised. The decision should be discussed with a qualified breast surgical team.

items.q: What is the main difference between the two surgeries?
items.a: The main difference is how much breast tissue is removed: breast-conserving surgery keeps most of the breast, while a mastectomy removes it entirely. Breast-conserving surgery is usually paired with radiation, whereas some mastectomy patients may avoid radiation depending on their pathology. Both aim to remove the cancer completely. Which option is appropriate depends on cancer type, stage, breast size, and the treating team's assessment.

items.q: Is one surgery more effective at treating breast cancer?
items.a: For many patients with early-stage breast cancer, breast-conserving surgery with radiation and mastectomy offer broadly comparable long-term survival, based on decades of clinical studies. Neither is automatically "better" for everyone. Effectiveness depends on tumour biology, stage, margins, and whether all cancer is removed. The most suitable option should be decided with your oncology team after reviewing your imaging, pathology, and overall health.

items.q: Who is a good candidate for breast-conserving surgery?
items.a: Breast-conserving surgery may be suitable for selected patients with a single, relatively small tumour and enough healthy breast tissue to keep a natural shape after removal. Candidacy also depends on whether radiation can safely follow the operation. It may not be advised for very large tumours, multiple tumour areas, or certain genetic risks. Eligibility should be confirmed by the surgical and oncology team after full evaluation.

items.q: When is a mastectomy recommended instead?
items.a: A mastectomy may be recommended when the tumour is large relative to breast size, when cancer is present in more than one part of the breast, or when clear margins cannot be achieved with a lumpectomy. It may also be considered for certain inherited gene changes or when radiation is unsafe. This recommendation depends on individual factors and should be made by the treating medical team.

items.q: Does breast-conserving surgery always require radiation?
items.a: Breast-conserving surgery is usually followed by radiation therapy, which helps lower the chance of the cancer returning in the remaining breast tissue. In some carefully selected older patients or specific low-risk tumours, doctors may discuss adjusting or omitting radiation. This is decided case by case. If radiation cannot be given for medical reasons, a mastectomy may be considered instead. Your radiation oncologist can explain what applies to you.

items.q: What are the risks and side effects of each surgery?
items.a: Both surgeries carry general risks such as bleeding, infection, scarring, and changes in breast or arm sensation. Breast-conserving surgery may cause changes in breast shape and radiation-related effects like skin irritation or fatigue. Mastectomy is a larger operation with a longer recovery and greater impact on breast appearance unless reconstruction is done. Side effects vary by individual and should be discussed in detail with your surgical team.

items.q: How long is recovery after each type of surgery?
items.a: Recovery after breast-conserving surgery is often shorter, with many patients resuming daily activities within one to two weeks, though radiation adds several weeks of treatment. Mastectomy recovery is usually longer, commonly several weeks, and can be extended if reconstruction is performed. Individual recovery depends on the extent of surgery, healing, and overall health. Your surgical team can give a realistic timeline for your situation.

items.q: How much do breast cancer surgeries cost?
items.a: The cost of breast-conserving surgery or mastectomy varies widely by country, hospital, surgeon, and whether reconstruction or radiation is included. Breast-conserving surgery may appear less expensive upfront but usually adds the cost of radiation, while mastectomy with reconstruction can raise surgical costs. Final pricing depends on diagnosis, stage, tests, hospital stay, and complications. A hospital estimate should be requested before treatment for accurate figures.

items.q: Are both surgeries available in India?
items.a: Both breast-conserving surgery and mastectomy are widely available in India at many cancer hospitals, often with experienced breast surgical oncology teams and reconstruction options. Availability of advanced techniques, radiation, and reconstruction can vary between centres. International patients sometimes consider India for these procedures, though access depends on hospital acceptance, medical review, and travel arrangements. Specific options should be confirmed directly with the chosen hospital.

items.q: Which countries offer advanced breast cancer surgery?
items.a: Advanced breast cancer surgery, including oncoplastic and reconstructive techniques, is offered in many countries such as India, Turkey, Germany, the United States, and several others with established cancer centres. The quality, waiting times, and cost differ between locations. Choosing where to have surgery should depend on tumour needs, surgeon experience, follow-up care, and personal circumstances, and is best discussed with a qualified oncology team.

items.q: Does insurance usually cover these surgeries?
items.a: Many health insurance plans cover breast cancer surgery, but coverage for radiation, reconstruction, and follow-up varies by policy and country. Some plans fully cover mastectomy and reconstruction, while others have limits or require pre-approval. International patients often pay out of pocket or use specific medical travel arrangements. Because coverage differs, patients should confirm details with their insurer and hospital before treatment rather than assume full coverage.

items.q: Can I have breast reconstruction after a mastectomy?
items.a: Breast reconstruction is available for many patients after a mastectomy and can be done at the same time as surgery or later. Options include implant-based reconstruction or using the patient's own tissue, each with different recovery and results. Suitability depends on health, cancer treatment plan, and whether radiation is needed. Reconstruction choices should be discussed with a breast and plastic surgical team before deciding on surgery.

items.q: What is oncoplastic breast-conserving surgery?
items.a: Oncoplastic surgery combines cancer removal with plastic surgery techniques to reshape the breast during breast-conserving surgery, aiming for better cosmetic results while removing the tumour safely. It may allow some patients to keep their breast even when a larger area needs removal. This approach may be suitable for selected patients and depends on tumour size, breast shape, and surgeon expertise, as determined by the surgical team.

items.q: Are clinical trials available for breast cancer surgery?
items.a: Clinical trials in breast cancer sometimes study surgical techniques, margins, radiation timing, or combinations with other treatments. Taking part is optional and does not guarantee benefit or enrolment, as trials have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Eligibility is decided after medical record review and investigator assessment. Patients interested in trials should ask their oncology team whether any suitable studies are open at their treatment centre.

items.q: How do I decide between the two surgeries?
items.a: Deciding between breast-conserving surgery and mastectomy involves weighing tumour size and location, breast size, the need for radiation, genetic risk, and your own preferences about appearance and peace of mind. There is often no single right answer, and both can be safe options for early breast cancer. The best decision is made together with your surgical and oncology team after reviewing your full medical picture.

items.q: Can international patients travel abroad for breast cancer surgery?
items.a: International patients can travel abroad for breast cancer surgery, but access depends on hospital acceptance, medical record review, visa approval, travel fitness, and overall condition. Timely treatment is important in cancer care, so planning should account for possible delays. Patients usually need recent imaging, pathology, and reports for review before travel. It is wise to confirm the full treatment and follow-up plan with the receiving hospital in advance.

items.q: What medical reports are needed to plan surgery abroad?
items.a: To plan breast cancer surgery abroad, hospitals typically request recent mammograms, ultrasound or MRI images, biopsy and pathology reports, hormone receptor and HER2 status, and a summary of overall health and any previous treatment. Additional tests may be requested after review. Having complete, up-to-date reports helps specialists give accurate advice and cost estimates. Requirements vary by hospital, so confirm the exact list with the treating centre.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with choosing breast cancer surgery?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centres, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health. This support is intended to make comparing breast-conserving surgery and mastectomy options clearer, not to replace medical advice from your doctors.
